families.s: HSE artificial optical-radiation, ultraviolet and laser guidance
families.t: UV, visible and infrared radiation, hazardous sources, eye and skin injury, assessment, engineering controls, work practices, training and PPE
f: Optical radiation includes ultraviolet, visible and infrared radiation.
Solar UV can damage eyes and skin and can contribute to skin cancer.
Powerful lasers can cause serious eye injury, blindness and skin burns.
The artificial optical radiation regulations protect workers from hazardous artificial sources.
Most workplaces are already adequately protected, but hazardous sources require proportionate assessment and control.
Exposure should be reduced as low as reasonably practicable where hazardous artificial sources are used.
Engineering enclosure, interlocks, screens and controlled access are preferred before reliance on PPE.
Workers need information, training and eye or skin protection matched to the source and task.
families.g: Optical-radiation risk depends on wavelength, power, beam geometry, exposure time, reflections, distance, enclosure, access, eye and skin exposure and protective equipment.

families.s: HSE ionising-radiation exposure, authorisation and protection guidance
families.t: X-rays, gamma and radioactive materials, risk assessment, ALARP, engineering controls, dose limits, notification, registration, consent and incident reporting
f: Ionising radiation includes X-rays, gamma rays and radiation from radioactive substances.
People can be exposed externally or through inhalation, ingestion or contamination of wounds.
Employers must assess radiation risks and protect workers and the public.
Exposure should be kept as low as reasonably practicable and below specified dose limits.
Engineering controls and design features should be used before safe systems and PPE.
Low-, medium- and high-risk practices may require notification, registration or consent respectively.
An authorised person familiar with the employer's practices should submit regulatory information.
Relevant radiation incidents and material changes must be reported or managed under the applicable requirements.
families.g: Ionising-radiation risk depends on source type and activity, energy, shielding, distance, time, contamination route, work practice, authorisation, monitoring and emergency arrangements.

families.s: HSE workplace radon assessment, testing and control guidance
families.t: affected areas, underground workplaces, measurement, 300 Bq/m3 threshold, notification, engineering controls, remeasurement and RPA advice
f: Radon is a radioactive gas that cannot be seen, smelled or tasted and requires measurement.
Employers must review the potential radon hazard in their workplaces.
Ground-floor, basement and underground workplaces can have elevated radon levels.
Workplaces in radon-affected areas should normally be tested unless a detailed assessment justifies otherwise.
Annual average concentrations above 300 Bq/m3 can trigger notification and additional exposure controls.
Controls can include ventilation, sealing ground-contact gaps, positive ventilation or radon sumps.
Radon levels should be remeasured after engineered controls to verify effectiveness.
A radiation protection adviser with radon experience may be needed for exposure management.
families.g: Radon risk depends on geology, building construction, floor level, ventilation, occupancy, seasonal variation, measured concentration, remediation performance and review frequency.

families.s: HSE legionella risk-assessment and responsible-person guidance
families.t: water-system understanding, 20–45°C range, storage, aerosols, nutrients, susceptible people, competent responsibility, contractors and review
f: The dutyholder is responsible for identifying and assessing foreseeable legionella exposure risks.
The assessment should describe the water system, responsibilities, risk sources, controls, monitoring and review.
Risk factors include water temperatures between 20 and 45°C, storage or recirculation, nutrients and biofilm.
Systems producing and dispersing droplets can expose people to contaminated aerosols.
Age, illness or weakened immunity can increase susceptibility.
A competent responsible person should have authority, skills, system knowledge and experience.
Using a contractor does not remove the dutyholder's responsibility to ensure the work is adequate.
The assessment should be reviewed when systems, occupancy, controls or other relevant conditions change.
families.g: Legionella risk depends on system type, temperature, stagnation, nutrients, aerosol generation, susceptible occupants, control performance, maintenance, competence and review.

families.s: HSE legionella written-control-scheme, temperature and monitoring guidance
families.t: written scheme, system schematic, temperature control, stagnation, cleanliness, treatment, monitoring, records and effectiveness review
f: Where risk is identified, a written control scheme should describe the system, responsibilities, operation and checks.
Water spray should be controlled and conditions favouring legionella growth should be avoided.
Stagnation should be reduced by avoiding unnecessary pipe lengths and removing redundant pipework.
Systems should be kept clean and treated where necessary to control microbial growth.
Cold water should generally be kept below 20°C where possible.
Hot water should generally be stored at least at 60°C and reach target distribution temperatures promptly.
Control measures should be monitored and maintenance, checks and corrective actions recorded.
The written scheme and controls should be reviewed to confirm they remain effective.
families.g: Control effectiveness depends on system design, temperatures, flow and stagnation, cleanliness, treatment, aerosol control, monitoring accuracy, records, maintenance and corrective action.
